summary: This document defines a framework for energy management of devices in or attached to communication networks. It describes a physical reference model and an information model built around Energy Objects, which have identity, classification and context and can be monitored or controlled.

plainLanguage.summary: Your house has a meter that shows how much power things use. This RFC describes a way for network gadgets to report and manage their own power use in a common way.

questions: how to monitor power in network devices
subtitle: Framework for monitoring and controlling power use in networked devices.

tldr.problem: Network devices and components consume significant power, but managing that consumption requires a common vocabulary and data model that IT management systems understand.
tldr.mechanism: Defines a framework with Energy Objects (devices, components, power interfaces) that can be monitored for power, energy, and demand, and controlled by changing their power states.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can now use standard management tools to measure and control power across routers, servers, switches, and other equipment.

today: RFC 7326 is an Informational framework from 2014 that has not been obsoleted. It forms the basis for YANG data models and MIB modules used in real network management systems to monitor power in data centers and networks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Energy management has become a critical concern for organizations running networks. Traditional network management focuses on faults, configuration, accounting, performance, and security (FCAPS), but energy use is now essential. This document defines a framework for Energy Management (EMAN) that extends management systems to monitor and control power.

The framework covers devices within or attached to communication networks, such as routers, switches, servers, and even power distribution units (PDUs). It also covers components within devices, such as line cards or power supplies. Devices can be consumers of energy, producers (like solar panels), or both.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks use a lot of electricity. This framework lets network managers track and control that power use the same way they track other network properties.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
The framework introduces several key ideas. An Energy Object is an abstract representation of any device or component that produces, consumes, or stores energy. There are three types: Devices (physical equipment like a router), Components (parts of devices like a fan or power supply), and Power Interfaces (the connections where energy flows in or out, like a power inlet).

Power is the instantaneous rate of energy transfer (in watts), while energy is power accumulated over time (in watt-hours). Demand is the average power over a time interval. Power States describe modes like on, off, sleep, or standby. A device in a lower power state uses less energy than the same device in a higher power state.

Power Attributes measure the electrical characteristics where energy is provided or consumed: current, voltage, frequency, and phase. These are important for understanding the quality of the power supply itself.
sections.plainLanguage: An energy object is any device or part of a device. It can do three things: you measure its power (how much electricity right now), its energy (how much total so far), and its state (on, off, asleep). Power attributes tell you about the electricity quality.

sections.title: The Information Model
sections.content:
The framework organizes Energy Objects with several categories of information. Identity includes a unique identifier (UUID) and an optional human-readable name. Context describes the object's role and importance: what category it is (consumer, producer, meter), its importance to business operations (1-100 scale), keywords for grouping, its role (e.g., "Faculty Desktop"), and which Energy Management Domain it belongs to (often a metered section of a building).

Measurement attributes record present power, power attributes, cumulative energy consumed or produced, and demand over time intervals. Control attributes specify what Power States the device supports and allow setting the desired state. Relationships model how devices connect through their power interfaces: power source relationships (who supplies whom), metering relationships (which meter measures which device), and aggregation relationships (who collects data from whom).
sections.plainLanguage: Each energy object has an identity (name and ID), context (what it does and how important), measurements (power and energy), control (turn it on/off/low-power), and relationships (who powers it, who measures it).

sections.title: Power States and Control
sections.content:
Devices support Power State Sets, which are collections of named power states. The framework supports three major standards: IEEE1621 (simple: on, sleep, off), DMTF (15 states for computers following ACPI standards), and EMAN (12 states: 6 operational and 6 non-operational).

EMAN states range from mechoff (completely powered down, no wake-up capability) through softoff, hibernate, sleep, standby, and ready (waiting to wake), then into operational states like lowMinus and low (reduced functionality), medium, high, and maximumPower (full capability). Each state has different power consumption and responsiveness characteristics.

Control allows setting a device to a desired Power State. The device transitions to that state and reports when the transition completes. Statistics track time spent in each state and the number of transitions, helping operators understand device behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: Devices can be turned on, off, or into low-power modes. Different standards define different numbers of modes. The framework lets you ask a device to go into a mode and tracks how long it stays there.

sections.title: Relationships and Aggregation
sections.content:
Energy Objects have relationships that model the physical power network. A power source relationship indicates that one device or component provides power to another: a PDU provides power to a server, a server provides power to its components. A metering relationship indicates that one device measures the power of another: an electrical meter measures a PDU or building's total consumption. An aggregation relationship indicates that one object collects and sums measurements from others: a network management system might aggregate power measurements from all devices in a building.

These relationships enable the management system to understand the power topology, separate from the network topology. For example, two servers might be on the same network switch but powered from different PDUs. The framework lets you query the power distribution tree independently.
sections.plainLanguage: Devices connect to power supplies, power supplies connect to meters, and management systems collect data from many meters. These connections are tracked so the system understands who powers whom and who measures what.

sections.title: Scope and Deployment
sections.content:
The framework applies to electrical equipment (routers, servers, cooling systems, power supplies) but not to purely mechanical equipment. It focuses on measuring and controlling power, not on energy procurement or environmental impact accounting. Target devices include simple appliances, computers, network equipment, components like line cards, batteries, renewable energy systems, Power over Ethernet endpoints, power distribution units, and devices that talk to building management systems.

The framework is neutral about what communications protocol carries the information. The Energy Objects can be modeled in SNMP MIB modules, YANG data models, REST APIs, or other management protocols. This allows deployment in any network management ecosystem.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework works for any electrical network device and any management protocol. It does not handle the business side of energy (billing, carbon accounting) or mechanical equipment, just electrical power measurement and control.
